title: Anthropic uses inquiry to claim current copyright law makes AI training "impossible"
source_used: The Sydney Morning Herald; Journal Arta
key_facts: Anthropic and OpenAI appeared before the Australian parliament's Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence in Sydney on Tuesday 6 Oct 2026.
Jeff Bleich, Anthropic's international special envoy and former US ambassador to Australia, said it is technically impossible to 'license the entire internet'.
He said training in Australia could be found illegal under existing law without a licence from every rights holder.
He urged Australia to host advanced AI training 'under its own laws, with its own conditions attached'.
Journal Arta quotes him saying Anthropic had 'never tried to dictate to Australia' on copyright.
Groups for about 128,000 songwriters and over 40,000 authors and artists, including APRA AMCOS, told the committee AI firms must pay to train on Australian work.
Lawmakers are examining whether rights holders should have to opt out before their work is used for training.
quote_evidence: Under questioning, he said it was technically impossible to "license the entire internet", and that training in Australia could be found illegal under existing law without a licence from every rights holder.

At a parliamentary hearing in Sydney on Tuesday, Anthropic said it had not tried to dictate Australia's approach, while arguing that the current rules make training AI models in the country "impossible."
why_it_matters_hint: The hearing puts an AI company's copyright demand against creators' groups while Australia prepares AI laws.
